bio-473.subject: biology
bio-473.question: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria originated from an ancient symbiotic relationship. Which evidence BEST supports this theory?
options: Mitochondria contain actin filaments identical to those of bacteria
Mitochondria have a single membrane like gram-positive bacteria
Mitochondria are found in all prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and reproduce by binary fission
bio-473.explanation:
Correct Answer: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and reproduce by binary fission

The endosymbiotic theory (Lynn Margulis, 1967) states that mitochondria originated from alpha-proteobacteria engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells. Key evidence includes: (1) circular DNA without histones (like bacteria), (2) 70S ribosomes (bacterial type, not the 80S found in eukaryotic cytoplasm), (3) replication by binary fission (independent of the cell cycle), and (4) double membrane (the inner membrane from the original bacterium, the outer from the host's engulfing vesicle).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Mitochondria contain actin filaments identical to those of bacteria: Mitochondria do not contain actin filaments. The cytoskeleton (including actin) is a feature of the eukaryotic cytoplasm, not of mitochondria. Furthermore, bacteria have the actin homolog MreB, but it is structurally distinct from eukaryotic actin.

B. Mitochondria have a single membrane, but mitochondria actually have a double membrane similar to gram-negative bacteria: Mitochondria have a DOUBLE membrane, not a single membrane. The double membrane is itself evidence for endosymbiosis - the inner membrane corresponds to the ancestral bacterium's plasma membrane, and the outer membrane corresponds to the host cell's engulfing vesicle.

C. Mitochondria are found in all prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells: Mitochondria are NOT found in prokaryotes. They are exclusively a eukaryotic organelle. Some eukaryotes (like Giardia) have reduced mitochondrial remnants (mitosomes), but no prokaryote contains mitochondria.

Key Educational Points:

FeatureMitochondriaBacteriaEukaryotic cytoplasm
DNA shapeCircularCircularLinear
Ribosomes70S70S80S
DivisionBinary fissionBinary fissionMitosis
MembranesDoubleSingle/DoubleN/A

Bottom Line: Mitochondria share circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and binary fission with bacteria, strongly supporting their endosymbiotic origin.

bio-474.subject: biology
bio-474.question: The earliest fossil evidence of life on Earth dates to approximately:
options: 3.5 billion years ago
4.6 billion years ago
2.1 billion years ago
540 million years ago
bio-474.explanation:
Correct Answer: 3.5 billion years ago

The earliest widely accepted fossil evidence of life comes from stromatolites (layered microbial mats) found in Western Australia, dating to approximately 3.5 billion years ago. Chemical evidence (carbon isotope ratios) from Greenland rocks suggests life may have existed as early as 3.7–3.8 billion years ago, but the oldest undisputed microfossils are ~3.5 billion years old.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. 4.6 billion years ago: 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth itself. During the first several hundred million years (the Hadean eon), conditions were too hostile for life - the surface was molten and subject to intense meteorite bombardment (Late Heavy Bombardment ended ~3.9 billion years ago).

C. 2.1 billion years ago: By 2.1 billion years ago, life was already well established. This date roughly corresponds to the earliest eukaryotic fossils (Grypania spiralis). Prokaryotic life existed for at least 1.4 billion years before eukaryotes appeared.

D. 540 million years ago: This is the approximate date of the Cambrian Explosion, when most major animal phyla appeared in the fossil record within a relatively short period. Life existed for roughly 3 billion years before this event.

Key Educational Points:

  • Earth formed ~4.6 Ga → earliest life ~3.5–3.8 Ga → oxygen accumulation ~2.4 Ga → eukaryotes ~2.1 Ga → Cambrian explosion ~540 Ma
  • Stromatolites are structures formed by cyanobacteria and are still found today (e.g., Shark Bay, Australia)
  • The time from Earth's formation to the first life was relatively short (~800 million years), suggesting that abiogenesis may occur readily under the right conditions

Bottom Line: The earliest fossil evidence of life (stromatolites) dates to ~3.5 billion years ago, roughly 1 billion years after Earth formed.

bio-475.subject: biology
bio-475.question: Which of the following is the correct sequence of events in chemical evolution leading to the first cells?
options: Formation of polymers → abiotic synthesis of monomers → formation of protobionts → origin of self-replicating molecules
Formation of protobionts → abiotic synthesis of monomers → formation of polymers → origin of self-replicating molecules
Origin of self-replicating molecules → abiotic synthesis of monomers → formation of protobionts → formation of polymers
Abiotic synthesis of monomers → formation of polymers → origin of self-replicating molecules → formation of protobionts
bio-475.explanation:
Correct Answer: Abiotic synthesis of monomers → formation of polymers → origin of self-replicating molecules → formation of protobionts

Chemical evolution followed a logical progression: (1) Simple inorganic molecules gave rise to organic monomers (amino acids, nucleotides, sugars) through abiotic synthesis driven by energy sources like lightning and UV radiation. (2) Monomers polymerized into more complex molecules (polypeptides, polynucleotides). (3) Self-replicating molecules (likely RNA) emerged, allowing information transfer. (4) These molecules became enclosed in membrane-bound protobionts, leading to primitive cells.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Formation of polymers → abiotic synthesis of monomers → ... This reverses the first two steps. Polymers are made FROM monomers, so monomers must form first. You cannot have polypeptides before amino acids exist.

A. Formation of protobionts → abiotic synthesis of monomers → ... Protobionts are structures composed of organic molecules. They cannot form before their molecular building blocks are synthesized. This reverses the entire logical sequence.

C. Origin of self-replicating molecules → abiotic synthesis of monomers → ... Self-replicating molecules (like RNA) are themselves polymers made of monomers (nucleotides). Monomers must be synthesized abiotically before complex self-replicating molecules can arise.

Key Educational Points:

  • Each step builds on the previous one - monomers → polymers → replication → compartmentalization
  • The transition from chemical evolution to biological evolution likely occurred when self-replicating systems became enclosed in membranes
  • Natural selection could begin operating once there were self-replicating entities with heritable variation

Bottom Line: Chemical evolution proceeded from simple monomers to polymers to self-replicating molecules to membrane-enclosed protobionts.

bio-476.subject: biology
bio-476.question: The deep-sea hydrothermal vent hypothesis for the origin of life proposes that life began near underwater volcanic vents. What advantage do these environments offer over the surface "primordial soup" model?
options: Hydrothermal vents provide oxygen-rich conditions ideal for aerobic metabolism
Hydrothermal vents contain large amounts of pre-formed DNA
Hydrothermal vents have lower temperatures that preserve fragile organic molecules
Hydrothermal vents supply continuous chemical energy and mineral catalysts in a protected environment
bio-476.explanation:
Correct Answer: Hydrothermal vents supply continuous chemical energy and mineral catalysts in a protected environment

Deep-sea hydrothermal vents (especially alkaline vents, or "white smokers") provide a continuous source of chemical energy from reduced compounds (H₂, H₂S, CH₄), mineral surfaces (iron-sulfur, nickel) that can catalyze reactions, and a protected environment shielded from UV radiation and meteorite impacts. The natural pH and temperature gradients across vent walls could have driven proto-metabolic reactions.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Hydrothermal vents provide oxygen-rich conditions ideal for aerobic metabolism: The deep ocean near hydrothermal vents was anoxic (oxygen-free) in early Earth. Aerobic metabolism evolved much later, after the Great Oxidation Event. The vent hypothesis actually relies on anaerobic chemistry, which is an advantage because oxygen would destroy prebiotic organic molecules.

B. Hydrothermal vents contain large amounts of pre-formed DNA: DNA is not found naturally in hydrothermal vent fluid. DNA is a biological molecule that is synthesized only by living organisms. The vent hypothesis proposes conditions for abiotic synthesis of simpler precursors, not pre-formed DNA.

C. Hydrothermal vents have lower temperatures that preserve fragile organic molecules: "Black smokers" can reach 350°C or higher, which would destroy organic molecules. However, alkaline vents ("white smokers") are cooler (~70–90°C), and the mixing zones between vent fluid and ocean water provide moderate temperature gradients. The claim of universally low temperatures is incorrect.

Key Educational Points:

  • Alkaline hydrothermal vents (Russell and Martin model) provide natural proton gradients similar to those used in modern chemiosmosis
  • Iron-sulfur minerals at vents can catalyze carbon fixation reactions
  • This model explains why modern enzymes often have iron-sulfur clusters at their active sites

Bottom Line: Deep-sea hydrothermal vents provide continuous chemical energy, mineral catalysts, and protection from harsh surface conditions - key advantages for the origin of life.

bio-477.subject: biology
bio-477.question: A ribozyme is a type of RNA molecule that can catalyze specific biochemical reactions. The discovery of ribozymes is significant because it:
options: proved that proteins were the first biological catalysts
demonstrated that DNA can function without RNA
supported the idea that RNA could have served as both genetic material and enzyme before DNA and proteins evolved
showed that all modern enzymes are made of RNA
bio-477.explanation:
Correct Answer: supported the idea that RNA could have served as both genetic material and enzyme before DNA and proteins evolved

The discovery of ribozymes by Thomas Cech (self-splicing introns in Tetrahymena, 1982) and Sidney Altman (RNase P, 1983) - for which they shared the 1989 Nobel Prize - provided crucial evidence for the RNA world hypothesis. If RNA can both store information and catalyze reactions, then a primitive RNA-based life form could have existed before the evolution of DNA (for information storage) and proteins (for catalysis).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Proved that proteins were the first biological catalysts: The discovery of ribozymes actually challenged the assumption that only proteins can be catalysts. It showed that RNA can also function as an enzyme, suggesting that proteins may NOT have been the first catalysts - RNA may have preceded them.

B. Demonstrated that DNA can function without RNA: Ribozyme discovery has nothing to do with DNA functioning without RNA. In fact, it suggests the opposite - that RNA was more functionally central in early life, and DNA came later as a more stable information storage molecule.

D. Showed that all modern enzymes are made of RNA: The vast majority of modern enzymes are proteins. Ribozymes are relatively rare in modern organisms, though they perform some critical functions (e.g., the ribosome's peptidyl transferase center is a ribozyme). The discovery showed RNA CAN be catalytic, not that all enzymes are RNA.

Key Educational Points:

  • Key ribozymes: self-splicing introns (Group I and II), RNase P, ribosomal RNA (peptidyl transferase)
  • Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman won the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ribozyme discovery
  • The ribosome is fundamentally a ribozyme - the catalytic core is rRNA, not protein

Bottom Line: Ribozymes demonstrate that RNA can catalyze reactions, supporting the RNA world hypothesis that RNA preceded both DNA and proteins in early life.

bio-478.subject: biology
bio-478.question: In the lac operon of E. coli, what happens when both glucose and lactose are ABSENT from the growth medium?
options: The operon is maximally transcribed due to CAP activation
The operon is transcribed at a low basal level only
RNA polymerase constitutively transcribes the structural genes
The repressor binds the operator and the operon is not transcribed
bio-478.explanation:
Correct Answer: The repressor binds the operator and the operon is not transcribed

When lactose is absent, there is no allolactose (the inducer) to bind and inactivate the lac repressor. The active repressor protein binds to the operator sequence, physically blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA). Even though glucose is also absent (meaning cAMP levels are high and CAP is active), the repressor's block at the operator prevents transcription.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The operon is maximally transcribed due to CAP activation: While it is true that low glucose leads to high cAMP, which activates the CAP-cAMP complex, CAP activation alone is not sufficient for transcription. The repressor must also be removed from the operator by the inducer (allolactose). Both conditions - CAP activation AND inducer presence - are required for maximal transcription.

B. The operon is transcribed at a low basal level only: Some very low-level "leaky" transcription may occur in reality (to produce the small amount of permease needed to initially transport lactose into the cell), but the standard model states that repressor binding effectively blocks transcription. For exam purposes, the operon is considered OFF when the repressor is bound.

C. RNA polymerase constitutively transcribes the structural genes: The lac operon is an inducible operon, meaning it is OFF by default and turned ON only when needed (when lactose is present). Constitutive expression would occur only if there were a mutation in the repressor gene or the operator.

Key Educational Points:

Glucose only+−LowNoYesOFF
Lactose only−+HighYesNoMAXIMAL
Both present++LowNoNoLOW

Bottom Line: Without lactose, the lac repressor remains active and blocks transcription regardless of glucose status.

bio-479.subject: biology
bio-479.question: The trp operon in E. coli is regulated by a mechanism called attenuation. What does attenuation involve?
options: A repressor protein that binds the operator only when tryptophan is present
Activation of the operon by a tryptophan-CAP complex
Degradation of trp mRNA by RNase when tryptophan concentrations are low
Premature termination of mRNA transcription in the leader sequence when tryptophan levels are high
bio-479.explanation:
Correct Answer: Premature termination of mRNA transcription in the leader sequence when tryptophan levels are high

Attenuation is a regulatory mechanism unique to prokaryotes that uses the coupling of transcription and translation. The trp operon mRNA has a leader sequence (trpL) containing two tandem tryptophan codons. When tryptophan is abundant, charged tRNAᵀʳᵖ is plentiful, the ribosome translates through these codons quickly, and the mRNA folds into a terminator hairpin structure (3:4 hairpin), causing RNA polymerase to dissociate before transcribing the structural genes.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A repressor protein that binds the operator only when tryptophan is present: This describes corepression, which is a separate regulatory mechanism of the trp operon (the trp repressor requires tryptophan as a corepressor to bind the operator). Attenuation is an additional, distinct layer of control that operates at the level of mRNA secondary structure, not repressor-operator binding.

B. Activation of the operon by a tryptophan-CAP complex: CAP (catabolite activator protein) is involved in regulating the lac operon and other sugar metabolism operons in response to glucose levels. CAP does not regulate the trp operon. The trp operon is regulated by the trp repressor and attenuation.

C. Degradation of trp mRNA by RNase when tryptophan concentrations are low: mRNA degradation by RNases is a general mechanism of gene regulation, but it is not what attenuation refers to. Attenuation specifically involves early termination of transcription, not post-transcriptional degradation of completed mRNA.

Key Educational Points:

  • Attenuation works because prokaryotes couple transcription and translation (no nuclear envelope separating the two)
  • The trp operon has TWO regulatory mechanisms: corepression (operator level) and attenuation (leader sequence level)
  • When tryptophan is LOW, the ribosome stalls at trp codons → anti-terminator hairpin (2:3) forms → transcription continues
  • Attenuation cannot occur in eukaryotes because transcription (nucleus) and translation (cytoplasm) are spatially separated

Bottom Line: Attenuation regulates the trp operon by causing premature transcription termination when tryptophan levels are high, using mRNA secondary structure changes.

bio-480.subject: biology
bio-480.question: In bacterial conjugation, what is the role of the F plasmid?
options: It encodes the genes for pilus formation and DNA transfer from donor (F+) to recipient (F−)
It encodes antibiotic resistance genes that are transferred to the recipient
It integrates into the bacterial chromosome and prevents further conjugation
It carries the genes for restriction enzymes that protect against phage DNA
bio-480.explanation:
Correct Answer: It encodes the genes for pilus formation and DNA transfer from donor (F+) to recipient (F−)

The F (fertility) plasmid carries the tra genes that encode the sex pilus (F pilus) and the DNA transfer machinery. During conjugation, the F+ (donor) cell extends its pilus to contact an F− (recipient) cell, forming a cytoplasmic bridge. A single strand of the F plasmid is transferred to the recipient, which then synthesizes the complementary strand and becomes F+.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. It encodes antibiotic resistance genes that are transferred to the recipient: Antibiotic resistance genes are carried on R plasmids (resistance plasmids), not the F plasmid. While the F plasmid enables the conjugation machinery, it is the R plasmid that carries resistance genes. However, R plasmids can sometimes also carry transfer genes (tra genes) or be co-transferred with F plasmids.

C. It integrates into the bacterial chromosome and prevents further conjugation: The F plasmid CAN integrate into the chromosome (forming an Hfr strain), but this does NOT prevent conjugation. Hfr cells actually transfer chromosomal DNA to F− recipients very efficiently, though the entire F plasmid is rarely transferred completely (so recipients usually remain F−).

D. It carries the genes for restriction enzymes that protect against phage DNA: Restriction enzymes are encoded by the bacterial chromosome, not by the F plasmid. The restriction-modification system is a bacterial defense against bacteriophages and is unrelated to conjugation.

Key Educational Points:

  • F+ × F− → both become F+ (F plasmid transferred)
  • Hfr × F− → recipient gets chromosomal genes but usually remains F− (incomplete F transfer)
  • F' (F prime) plasmid = excised F plasmid carrying some chromosomal genes → can transfer specific chromosomal genes to F− (sexduction)

Bottom Line: The F plasmid encodes the sex pilus and transfer machinery needed for bacterial conjugation from F+ donor to F− recipient.

bio-481.subject: biology
bio-481.question: During generalized transduction, how does bacterial DNA get transferred from one bacterium to another?
options: A bacteriophage accidentally packages random fragments of host bacterial DNA instead of its own genome
Two bacterial cells exchange DNA through direct cell-to-cell contact via a pilus
A bacterium takes up free DNA from the environment released by a lysed cell
A specialized phage excises a specific bacterial gene adjacent to its integration site
bio-481.explanation:
Correct Answer: A bacteriophage accidentally packages random fragments of host bacterial DNA instead of its own genome

In generalized transduction, during the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage, the host bacterial chromosome is degraded into fragments. Occasionally, a phage head mistakenly packages a random fragment of bacterial DNA instead of phage DNA. When this defective phage particle infects a new bacterium, it injects the bacterial DNA from the previous host, which can then be incorporated into the new host's chromosome by homologous recombination.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Two bacterial cells exchange DNA through direct cell-to-cell contact via a pilus: This describes conjugation, not transduction. Conjugation requires physical contact between cells through a sex pilus encoded by the F plasmid. Transduction uses bacteriophages as vectors and does not involve direct cell contact.

C. A bacterium takes up free DNA from the environment released by a lysed cell: This describes transformation, the process discovered by Frederick Griffith (1928) and confirmed by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944). In transformation, competent bacteria take up naked DNA from the environment. No phage is involved.

D. A specialized phage excises a specific bacterial gene adjacent to its integration site: This describes specialized transduction, not generalized transduction. In specialized transduction, a lysogenic phage (like lambda) imprecisely excises from the chromosome and takes nearby bacterial genes (e.g., gal or bio genes flanking the lambda attachment site). Only specific genes can be transferred, not random fragments.

Key Educational Points:

FeatureGeneralized transductionSpecialized transduction
Phage cycleLyticLysogenic (imprecise excision)
Genes transferredAny random geneOnly genes near phage integration site
MechanismAccidental packaging of host DNAImprecise excision carries adjacent genes
Example phageP1, P22Lambda (λ)

Bottom Line: Generalized transduction occurs when a phage accidentally packages random bacterial DNA during the lytic cycle and transfers it to a new host.

bio-482.subject: biology
bio-482.question: An R plasmid is clinically significant because it:
options: carries genes for antibiotic resistance that can be transferred between bacteria
enables bacteria to undergo meiosis
encodes the enzymes for lactose metabolism
is required for bacterial binary fission
bio-482.explanation:
Correct Answer: carries genes for antibiotic resistance that can be transferred between bacteria

R plasmids (resistance plasmids) carry genes encoding enzymes that inactivate antibiotics (e.g., beta-lactamases that break down penicillin), efflux pumps, or modified target sites. These plasmids can be transferred between bacteria via conjugation, even between different species, contributing to the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance - a major global health concern.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Enables bacteria to undergo meiosis: Bacteria are prokaryotes and NEVER undergo meiosis. Meiosis is exclusive to sexually reproducing eukaryotes. Bacteria reproduce by binary fission and exchange genetic material through conjugation, transformation, and transduction - none of which involves meiosis.

C. Encodes the enzymes for lactose metabolism: Lactose metabolism genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) are encoded in the lac operon on the bacterial chromosome, not on a plasmid. The lac operon is a chromosomal gene cluster, not a plasmid-borne system.

D. Is required for bacterial binary fission: Binary fission is the standard mode of bacterial reproduction and requires only the chromosomal DNA and cell division machinery. No plasmid is required for binary fission. Plasmids are extra-chromosomal DNA elements that provide accessory functions but are not essential for basic cell division.

Key Educational Points:

  • R plasmids are a major driver of the antibiotic resistance crisis
  • A single R plasmid can carry resistance genes for multiple antibiotics simultaneously (multi-drug resistance)
  • R plasmids can transfer between species (e.g., from E. coli to Salmonella), making resistance spread unpredictable
  • Overuse of antibiotics selects for bacteria carrying R plasmids

Bottom Line: R plasmids carry transferable antibiotic resistance genes that spread between bacteria via conjugation, posing a major clinical threat.

bio-483.subject: biology
bio-483.question: Transposons ("jumping genes") in bacteria are significant because they:
options: can move from one location to another in the genome, sometimes carrying antibiotic resistance genes
are required for normal DNA replication in all bacteria
replace the function of RNA polymerase during transcription
are only found in eukaryotic genomes and not in prokaryotes
bio-483.explanation:
Correct Answer: can move from one location to another in the genome, sometimes carrying antibiotic resistance genes

Transposons are mobile genetic elements (discovered by Barbara McClintock in maize) that can "jump" from one position to another within the genome or between the chromosome and plasmids. In bacteria, complex transposons often carry antibiotic resistance genes flanked by insertion sequences (IS elements). Transposition can disrupt genes, activate nearby genes, or spread resistance genes between the chromosome and plasmids.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Are required for normal DNA replication in all bacteria: Transposons are not part of the normal DNA replication machinery. DNA replication requires DNA polymerase III (and I), helicase, primase, ligase, and other replication proteins encoded by chromosomal genes. Transposons are accessory elements and many bacteria function perfectly well without them.

C. Replace the function of RNA polymerase during transcription: Transposons do not participate in transcription. They encode transposase (the enzyme that catalyzes their movement) and sometimes carry accessory genes, but they do not replace core transcription machinery.

D. Are only found in eukaryotic genomes and not in prokaryotes: Transposons are found in BOTH prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Barbara McClintock discovered them in eukaryotes (maize), but they are abundant in bacteria as well. Bacterial insertion sequences (IS elements) are the simplest transposons.

Key Educational Points:

  • Simple transposons (IS elements) = transposase gene flanked by inverted repeats
  • Complex transposons = carry additional genes (often antibiotic resistance) between two IS elements
  • Transposons create target site duplications when they insert
  • Barbara McClintock received the 1983 Nobel Prize for discovering transposons

Bottom Line: Transposons are mobile genetic elements that can move within genomes and often carry antibiotic resistance genes in bacteria.

bio-484.subject: biology
bio-484.question: In bacterial transformation, competence refers to:
options: the ability of a bacteriophage to integrate its DNA into the host chromosome
the ability of a transposon to move between chromosomal locations
the ability of a plasmid to replicate independently of the chromosome
the ability of a bacterium to take up exogenous DNA from its environment
bio-484.explanation:
Correct Answer: the ability of a bacterium to take up exogenous DNA from its environment

Competence is the physiological state in which a bacterial cell can take up naked (free) DNA from the surrounding environment. Some bacteria are naturally competent (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Bacillus subtilis), possessing specialized surface proteins that bind and import DNA. Other bacteria can be made artificially competent in the laboratory using CaCl₂ treatment, heat shock, or electroporation.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The ability of a bacteriophage to integrate its DNA into the host chromosome: This describes lysogeny, the process by which a temperate bacteriophage (like lambda phage) integrates its genome into the host chromosome to form a prophage. This is a phage property, not a bacterial competence mechanism.

B. The ability of a transposon to move between chromosomal locations: Transposition is mediated by the transposase enzyme encoded by the transposon itself. This is a property of the mobile genetic element, not a state of the bacterial cell, and it has nothing to do with competence for transformation.

C. The ability of a plasmid to replicate independently of the chromosome: This is a fundamental property of all plasmids - they have their own origin of replication (ori) that allows autonomous replication. This is unrelated to transformation or competence.

Key Educational Points:

  • Griffith's experiment (1928): demonstrated transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae (smooth → rough)
  • Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944): identified the transforming principle as DNA
  • Laboratory methods to induce competence: CaCl₂ + heat shock, electroporation
  • Only a small fraction of cells in a population may be naturally competent at any given time

Bottom Line: Competence is the ability of a bacterial cell to take up free DNA from its environment, enabling the process of transformation.

bio-485.subject: biology
bio-485.question: The lac operon contains three structural genes. Which of the following correctly identifies these genes and their products?
options: lacI (repressor), lacO (operator), lacP (promoter)
lacR (repressor), lacT (transacetylase), lacB (β-galactosidase)
lacZ (permease), lacY (β-galactosidase), lacA (repressor)
lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase)
bio-485.explanation:
Correct Answer: lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase)

The three structural genes of the lac operon are: (1) lacZ, encoding β-galactosidase - the enzyme that cleaves lactose into glucose and galactose; (2) lacY, encoding lactose permease - a membrane transport protein that brings lactose into the cell; and (3) lacA, encoding thiogalactoside transacetylase - which transfers an acetyl group to galactosides (its exact physiological role is less clear but may be involved in detoxification).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. lacI (repressor), lacO (operator), lacP (promoter): lacI, lacO, and lacP are indeed part of the lac operon system, but they are NOT structural genes. lacI is the regulatory gene (encodes the repressor protein), lacO is the operator (a DNA sequence, not a gene that encodes a protein), and lacP is the promoter (where RNA polymerase binds). Structural genes encode proteins with enzymatic or structural functions.

B. lacR (repressor), lacT (transacetylase), lacB (β-galactosidase): These gene names are incorrect. The lac operon genes are designated with specific letters: Z (β-galactosidase), Y (permease), A (transacetylase), and I (repressor). There are no genes named lacR, lacT, or lacB in the standard lac operon nomenclature.

C. lacZ (permease), lacY (β-galactosidase), lacA (repressor): This switches the products of lacZ and lacY. lacZ encodes β-galactosidase (not permease), and lacY encodes permease (not β-galactosidase). Additionally, the repressor is encoded by lacI, not lacA.

Key Educational Points:

  • All three structural genes are transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA
  • β-galactosidase also converts lactose to allolactose - the actual inducer of the operon
  • The lacI gene is transcribed constitutively from its own promoter, separate from the lac operon structural genes

Bottom Line: The lac operon's three structural genes are lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), and lacA (transacetylase), transcribed as one polycistronic mRNA.

bio-486.subject: biology
bio-486.question: In negative gene regulation, how is transcription typically controlled?
options: An activator protein binds the promoter to stimulate RNA polymerase binding
Transcription is always on and cannot be turned off
A repressor protein binds the operator to block transcription, and transcription occurs when the repressor is removed
Small RNA molecules degrade mRNA before it can be translated
bio-486.explanation:
Correct Answer: A repressor protein binds the operator to block transcription, and transcription occurs when the repressor is removed

In negative gene regulation, the default state is that a repressor protein binds to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the downstream genes. Transcription is "turned on" by removing the repressor - either through an inducer (as in the lac operon, where allolactose inactivates the repressor) or by depleting a corepressor (as in the trp operon, where lack of tryptophan leaves the repressor inactive).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. An activator protein binds the promoter to stimulate RNA polymerase binding: This describes POSITIVE gene regulation. In positive regulation, transcription requires an activator protein to help RNA polymerase bind. An example is the CAP-cAMP complex, which binds upstream of the lac operon promoter and enhances RNA polymerase recruitment when glucose is low.

B. Transcription is always on and cannot be turned off: This describes constitutive gene expression, not regulated gene expression. Most genes in bacteria are regulated, but some housekeeping genes (like those for ribosomal proteins) are expressed more or less constitutively.

D. Small RNA molecules degrade mRNA before it can be translated: This describes post-transcriptional regulation (e.g., RNA interference in eukaryotes or small regulatory RNAs in bacteria). While this is a real regulatory mechanism, it is not what defines negative gene regulation at the transcriptional level.

Key Educational Points:

TypeMechanismExample
Negative inducibleRepressor blocks transcription; inducer removes repressorlac operon (allolactose = inducer)
Negative repressibleRepressor alone is inactive; corepressor activates repressortrp operon (tryptophan = corepressor)
Positive regulationActivator enhances transcriptionCAP-cAMP at lac operon

Bottom Line: Negative gene regulation uses a repressor protein to block transcription; the gene is expressed only when the repressor is inactivated or removed.

bio-487.subject: biology
bio-487.question: An Hfr (High frequency recombination) strain of E. coli is formed when:
options: a bacterium acquires multiple copies of the same plasmid
the bacterial cell loses its cell wall and becomes a protoplast
a mutation inactivates the DNA mismatch repair system
the F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome
bio-487.explanation:
Correct Answer: the F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome

An Hfr strain is created when the F plasmid recombines into the bacterial chromosome via homologous recombination at IS (insertion sequence) elements shared between the F plasmid and chromosome. When an Hfr cell conjugates with an F− cell, it begins transferring the chromosomal DNA starting from the integrated F origin of transfer (oriT). Because the F genes are split across the end of the transferred DNA, the recipient usually does not receive the complete F plasmid and remains F−.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A bacterium acquires multiple copies of the same plasmid: Having multiple copies of a plasmid is called high copy number and is determined by the plasmid's origin of replication, not by chromosomal integration. The F plasmid is normally a low-copy-number plasmid (1-2 copies per cell). Multiple copies do not create an Hfr strain.

B. The bacterial cell loses its cell wall and becomes a protoplast: A protoplast (or spheroplast) is a bacterium that has lost its cell wall (e.g., by lysozyme treatment). This has no relationship to F plasmid biology or Hfr formation. Protoplasts are used in laboratory fusion experiments but are not a natural conjugation phenomenon.

C. A mutation inactivates the DNA mismatch repair system: Loss of mismatch repair leads to a mutator phenotype (increased mutation rate), not Hfr formation. Mismatch repair (e.g., MutS, MutL, MutH in E. coli) corrects replication errors. Its inactivation is associated with increased mutation frequency but has nothing to do with F plasmid integration.

Key Educational Points:

  • Hfr = F plasmid integrated into chromosome
  • Hfr × F− → chromosomal gene transfer; recipient usually stays F−
  • F' (F prime) = F plasmid excises imprecisely from chromosome, taking adjacent bacterial genes
  • Interrupted mating experiments use Hfr strains to map gene order on the bacterial chromosome

Bottom Line: An Hfr strain forms when the F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome, enabling high-frequency transfer of chromosomal genes during conjugation.

bio-488.subject: biology
bio-488.question: A newborn presents with severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, a high-pitched cry resembling a cat, and facial abnormalities. Which chromosomal abnormality is most consistent with these findings?
options: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (cri-du-chat syndrome)
Monosomy X (Turner syndrome)
bio-488.explanation:
Correct Answer: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (cri-du-chat syndrome)

Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm (p arm) of chromosome 5 (5p−). The hallmark feature is a distinctive high-pitched, mewing cry in infancy (resembling a cat, hence "cri du chat" - French for "cry of the cat"), caused by abnormal laryngeal development. Other features include microcephaly, intellectual disability, wide-set eyes, low-set ears, and a small jaw.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome): Edwards syndrome presents with clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia (small jaw), heart defects, and severe intellectual disability. The characteristic cat-like cry is NOT a feature of trisomy 18. Most affected infants die within the first year.

B. Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome): Patau syndrome features holoprosencephaly (failure of the forebrain to divide), cleft lip/palate, polydactyly (extra digits), microphthalmia (small eyes) or cyclopia, and heart defects. There is no cat-like cry. Most affected infants die within the first month.

D. Monosomy X (Turner syndrome): Turner syndrome (45,X) affects only females and presents with short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, lymphedema, coarctation of the aorta, and streak gonads. Intelligence is usually normal. There is no cat-like cry or microcephaly.

Key Educational Points:

  • Cri-du-chat = 5p deletion (remember: 5 letters in "chat" → chromosome 5)
  • The cat-like cry typically diminishes with age as the larynx develops
  • It is a structural chromosomal abnormality (deletion), not a numerical abnormality (aneuploidy)

Bottom Line: A high-pitched cat-like cry with microcephaly and intellectual disability is the classic presentation of cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion).

bio-489.subject: biology
bio-489.question: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Clenched fists with overlapping fingers
Rocker-bottom feet
Polydactyly and cleft lip/palate
Severe intellectual disability and heart defects
bio-489.explanation:
Correct Answer: Polydactyly and cleft lip/palate

Polydactyly (extra digits) and cleft lip/palate are characteristic features of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13), NOT Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18). Edwards syndrome is characterized by clenched fists with overlapping fingers (index finger overlaps the 3rd, and 5th overlaps the 4th), rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, prominent occiput, and severe congenital heart defects.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Clenched fists with overlapping fingers: This is a CLASSIC finding in Edwards syndrome. The distinctive pattern of overlapping fingers (2nd over 3rd, 5th over 4th) is highly characteristic and is an important clinical clue for prenatal and neonatal diagnosis.

B. Rocker-bottom feet: Rocker-bottom feet (a rounded convexity of the sole) is another hallmark of Edwards syndrome. The calcaneus is prominent and the sole appears rounded. This finding helps distinguish trisomy 18 from other chromosomal disorders.

D. Severe intellectual disability and heart defects: Both are present in Edwards syndrome. Virtually all affected individuals have severe intellectual disability. Congenital heart defects (especially ventricular septal defect, VSD) are present in over 90% of cases and are a major cause of early death.

Key Educational Points:

FeatureTrisomy 21 (Down)Trisomy 18 (Edwards)Trisomy 13 (Patau)
HandsSimian creaseClenched, overlapping fingersPolydactyly
FaceFlat face, epicanthal foldsSmall jaw, prominent occiputCleft lip/palate, microphthalmos
FeetSandal gapRocker-bottomRocker-bottom (also possible)
SurvivalInto adulthoodMedian ~10 daysMedian ~7 days

Bottom Line: Polydactyly and cleft lip/palate are features of trisomy 13 (Patau), not trisomy 18 (Edwards). Edwards syndrome features clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet.

bio-490.subject: biology
bio-490.question: A 17-year-old female presents with short stature, primary amenorrhea, a webbed neck, and widely spaced nipples on a broad chest. Her karyotype would most likely show:
options: 47,XXX
47,XXY
46,XX
bio-490.explanation:
Correct Answer: 45,X

This presentation is classic for Turner syndrome (45,X or 45,XO). Features include short stature (often < 5 feet), primary amenorrhea (due to streak gonads with no functional ovarian tissue), webbed neck (cystic hygroma remnant), shield chest with widely spaced nipples, coarctation of the aorta, horseshoe kidney, and lymphedema of hands and feet at birth. Intelligence is typically normal, though spatial reasoning may be affected.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 47,XXX (Triple X syndrome): Triple X females are typically tall, have normal fertility, and are often phenotypically normal. They may have mild learning difficulties, but they do NOT have short stature, webbed neck, or amenorrhea. Most 47,XXX women are never diagnosed because the phenotype is so mild.

B. 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome): This is a male condition. Affected individuals are phenotypically male (though with some female secondary characteristics) - tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, infertility, and often reduced body hair. The patient in this question is female, ruling out Klinefelter syndrome.

D. 46,XX (normal female): A normal female karyotype would not explain the constellation of short stature, primary amenorrhea, webbed neck, and shield chest. These findings strongly suggest a chromosomal abnormality, specifically monosomy X.

Key Educational Points:

  • Turner syndrome is the only viable monosomy in humans (all autosomal monosomies are lethal)
  • ~99% of 45,X conceptions end in spontaneous abortion; Turner syndrome is actually rare at birth
  • Mosaicism (45,X / 46,XX) is common and may produce a milder phenotype
  • Treatment includes growth hormone for short stature and estrogen replacement for puberty induction

Bottom Line: Short stature, primary amenorrhea, webbed neck, and shield chest in a female indicate Turner syndrome (45,X).

bio-491.subject: biology
bio-491.question: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is characterized by:
options: Tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, and infertility in males
Short stature, webbed neck, and ovarian dysgenesis in females
Polydactyly, cleft lip, and holoprosencephaly
Normal male phenotype with no clinical manifestations
bio-491.explanation:
Correct Answer: Tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, and infertility in males

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common sex chromosome disorder in males, occurring in approximately 1 in 600 male births. Key features include tall stature with long limbs, small firm testes, gynecomastia (breast development), infertility due to azoospermia (absence of sperm), reduced facial and body hair, and sometimes mild learning difficulties. Testosterone levels are reduced and FSH/LH are elevated.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Short stature, webbed neck, and ovarian dysgenesis in females: These are features of Turner syndrome (45,X), not Klinefelter syndrome. Turner affects females, while Klinefelter affects males. The key distinguishing features are the sex of the affected individual and the specific phenotypic findings.

C. Polydactyly, cleft lip, and holoprosencephaly: These are features of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13), an autosomal chromosome disorder. Polydactyly and midline defects are not associated with sex chromosome aneuploidies.

D. Normal male phenotype with no clinical manifestations: While Klinefelter syndrome can be mild (and some men are diagnosed only during infertility workup), it is NOT a completely normal phenotype. Most affected individuals have at least some clinical features, particularly small testes and infertility. About 64% of 47,XXY males are never diagnosed, however, because the features can be subtle.

Key Educational Points:

  • Most common cause of male hypogonadism and infertility
  • Extra X chromosome → Barr body present in male cells (normally males have 0 Barr bodies)
  • Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes minus 1
  • Risk of breast cancer is higher in Klinefelter males than in typical males (but still lower than in females)

Bottom Line: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents in males with tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, and infertility due to the extra X chromosome.

bio-492.subject: biology
bio-492.question: Nondisjunction during meiosis I versus meiosis II produces different patterns of aneuploidy. If nondisjunction occurs during meiosis I, what is the result?
options: Two normal gametes and two aneuploid gametes
Only one gamete is aneuploid; the other three are normal
All four gametes are normal
All four gametes are aneuploid - two with an extra chromosome and two missing a chromosome
bio-492.explanation:
Correct Answer: All four gametes are aneuploid - two with an extra chromosome and two missing a chromosome

When nondisjunction occurs in meiosis I, homologous chromosomes fail to separate during anaphase I. This means one secondary cell receives both homologs and the other receives none. After meiosis II proceeds normally, the result is four aneuploid gametes: two gametes with n+1 chromosomes and two gametes with n−1 chromosomes. None of the four gametes has a normal chromosome number.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Two normal gametes and two aneuploid gametes: This pattern occurs when nondisjunction happens in meiosis II, not meiosis I. In meiosis II nondisjunction, only one of the two secondary cells is affected. The unaffected cell produces two normal gametes, while the affected cell produces one n+1 and one n−1 gamete.

B. Only one gamete is aneuploid; the other three are normal: Nondisjunction always affects at least two gametes. The "lost" chromosome material from one cell must end up in another, so there are always complementary aneuploid products (n+1 paired with n−1).

C. All four gametes are normal: If nondisjunction occurred, at least some gametes must be aneuploid. Normal gamete production requires proper chromosome segregation at both meiotic divisions.

Key Educational Points:

FeatureNondisjunction in Meiosis INondisjunction in Meiosis II
What fails to separateHomologous chromosomesSister chromatids
Aneuploid gametes4 out of 4 (all)2 out of 4
Normal gametes02

Bottom Line: Nondisjunction in meiosis I produces four aneuploid gametes (all abnormal), while nondisjunction in meiosis II produces two normal and two aneuploid gametes.

bio-493.subject: biology
bio-493.question: The Philadelphia chromosome, associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), is formed by:
options: A reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, creating the BCR-ABL fusion gene
A deletion of the long arm of chromosome 22
Trisomy of chromosome 22
An inversion of the short arm of chromosome 9
bio-493.explanation:
Correct Answer: A reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, creating the BCR-ABL fusion gene

The Philadelphia chromosome results from a reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11), where part of the ABL1 proto-oncogene from chromosome 9 is fused with part of the BCR gene on chromosome 22. The resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene produces a constitutively active tyrosine kinase protein that drives uncontrolled cell proliferation. The shortened chromosome 22 carrying this fusion is called the Philadelphia chromosome.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. A deletion of the long arm of chromosome 22: While the Philadelphia chromosome appears shorter than normal chromosome 22 on karyotype, this is because of a translocation (exchange of segments), not a simple deletion. Material from chromosome 9 is added to 22, and material from 22 is added to 9 - it is a reciprocal exchange. A deletion would not create the critical BCR-ABL fusion gene.

C. Trisomy of chromosome 22: Trisomy 22 is not associated with CML. Trisomy refers to having three copies of a chromosome, which is a different type of chromosomal abnormality (numerical vs. structural). The Philadelphia chromosome involves a structural rearrangement.

D. An inversion of the short arm of chromosome 9: An inversion involves a segment of a chromosome being flipped 180°. The Philadelphia chromosome involves a translocation (exchange between two different chromosomes), not an inversion (rearrangement within a single chromosome).

Key Educational Points:

  • The Philadelphia chromosome was the first chromosomal abnormality linked to a specific cancer (1960)
  • BCR-ABL protein = constitutively active tyrosine kinase → uncontrolled growth of myeloid cells
  • Imatinib (Gleevec) specifically inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase - a landmark in targeted cancer therapy
  • Present in ~95% of CML cases and some cases of ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia)

Bottom Line: The Philadelphia chromosome is formed by t(9;22) reciprocal translocation creating the BCR-ABL fusion oncogene, the hallmark of CML.

bio-494.subject: biology
bio-494.question: Polyploidy refers to having more than two complete sets of chromosomes. Why is polyploidy generally lethal in humans but common in plants?
options: Human sex determination is disrupted by extra chromosome sets, and gene dosage imbalance is lethal, whereas plants tolerate polyploidy due to different sex determination and greater gene dosage tolerance
Plants have fewer chromosomes than humans, so extra sets are tolerated
Polyploidy causes cancer in all animals but not in plants
Humans are diploid while all plants are naturally polyploid
bio-494.explanation:
Correct Answer: Human sex determination is disrupted by extra chromosome sets, and gene dosage imbalance is lethal, whereas plants tolerate polyploidy due to different sex determination and greater gene dosage tolerance

In humans, polyploidy (3n or 4n) is nearly always lethal because: (1) the precise balance of sex chromosomes and autosomes is disrupted, causing abnormal sex determination; (2) gene dosage imbalance disrupts development; and (3) mitotic spindle formation is impaired with extra centrosomes. Plants, however, commonly tolerate polyploidy because they have more flexible sex determination, can self-fertilize, and many essential crop species are polyploid (wheat = hexaploid 6n, banana = triploid 3n).

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Plants have fewer chromosomes than humans: Many plants have more chromosomes than humans (e.g., fern Ophioglossum has over 1,200 chromosomes). The number of chromosomes is not the determining factor for polyploidy tolerance. It is about gene dosage balance and developmental flexibility.

C. Polyploidy causes cancer in all animals but not in plants: Polyploidy itself does not directly cause cancer. While some cancer cells are aneuploid or polyploid, polyploidy is not the cause of cancer - it is often a consequence of genomic instability in tumors. Normal polyploid cells exist in human tissues (e.g., hepatocytes, megakaryocytes) without being cancerous.

D. Humans are diploid while all plants are naturally polyploid: Not all plants are polyploid. Many plants are diploid (e.g., Arabidopsis thaliana, 2n = 10). However, polyploidy is far more common in plants than in animals, and many important crop species are polyploid as a result of natural or artificial hybridization events.

Key Educational Points:

  • Triploidy (69 chromosomes) in humans → spontaneous abortion or partial hydatidiform mole
  • Tetraploidy (92 chromosomes) in humans → almost always lethal before birth
  • Autopolyploidy = extra sets from the same species; allopolyploidy = sets from different species (common in plant speciation)

Bottom Line: Polyploidy is lethal in humans due to gene dosage and sex determination disruption, but is tolerated and even advantageous in many plant species.

bio-495.subject: biology
bio-495.question: A chromosomal inversion involves a segment of a chromosome being flipped 180°. What is the primary risk when an individual heterozygous for an inversion reproduces?
options: Crossing over within the inverted region during meiosis can produce unbalanced gametes with duplications and deletions
All offspring will have the same inversion
The inversion prevents all meiotic cell division entirely
Inversions always cause trisomy in offspring
bio-495.explanation:
Correct Answer: Crossing over within the inverted region during meiosis can produce unbalanced gametes with duplications and deletions

In a heterozygous inversion carrier, one chromosome has the normal gene order and the other has the inverted segment. During meiosis, when homologous chromosomes pair up, the inverted region forms a loop structure. If crossing over occurs within this loop, the resulting recombinant chromosomes can have duplications of some genes and deletions of others (unbalanced gametes). These unbalanced gametes typically lead to inviable embryos or offspring with severe abnormalities.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. All offspring will have the same inversion: Heterozygous inversion carriers can produce offspring who are: (1) normal homozygotes, (2) inversion heterozygotes like the parent, or (3) carry recombinant chromosomes (if crossing over occurred in the inverted segment). Not all offspring inherit the inversion.

C. The inversion prevents all meiotic cell division entirely: Inversions do NOT prevent meiosis. Meiosis proceeds normally - the chromosomes simply form an inversion loop during synapsis in meiosis I. The problem arises only if crossing over occurs within the inverted region, producing unbalanced recombinant chromosomes.

D. Inversions always cause trisomy in offspring: Inversions do not cause trisomy (which is a numerical chromosome abnormality caused by nondisjunction). Inversions cause structural problems - specifically duplications and deletions - if recombination occurs within the inverted segment. Trisomy and inversions are fundamentally different types of chromosomal abnormalities.

Key Educational Points:

  • Paracentric inversion = does not include centromere → crossover produces acentric and dicentric chromosomes
  • Pericentric inversion = includes centromere → crossover produces chromosomes with duplications and deletions
  • Inversion heterozygotes often have reduced fertility due to inviable recombinant gametes

Bottom Line: In inversion heterozygotes, crossing over within the inverted segment produces unbalanced gametes with duplications and deletions, often leading to inviable offspring.

bio-496.subject: biology
bio-496.question: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is associated with which of the following characteristic findings?
options: Holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, and cleft lip/palate
Single palmar crease (simian crease) and Brushfield spots on the iris
Clenched fists with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet
Tall stature, long limbs, and gynecomastia
bio-496.explanation:
Correct Answer: Holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, and cleft lip/palate

Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is characterized by severe midline defects including holoprosencephaly (failure of the prosencephalon to divide into two hemispheres), cleft lip and palate, polydactyly (extra digits, especially postaxial), microphthalmia (abnormally small eyes) or cyclopia in severe cases, omphalocele, and congenital heart defects. Median survival is approximately 7–10 days.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Single palmar crease (simian crease) and Brushfield spots on the iris: These are features of Down syndrome (trisomy 21). The single palmar crease (found in ~45% of Down syndrome) and Brushfield spots (speckled light-colored spots on the iris) are classic diagnostic clues for trisomy 21, not trisomy 13.

C. Clenched fists with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet: These are hallmark features of Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18). The characteristic hand posture (2nd finger overlapping 3rd, 5th overlapping 4th) is a useful clinical distinction from trisomy 13, which features polydactyly instead.

D. Tall stature, long limbs, and gynecomastia: These features describe Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), a sex chromosome disorder in males. Patau syndrome causes severe structural abnormalities incompatible with long-term survival, not growth pattern changes seen in sex chromosome aneuploidies.

Key Educational Points:

  • Trisomy 13 = midline defects (holoprosencephaly, cleft lip) + polydactyly + eye abnormalities
  • Remember "P" in Patau = "P"olydactyly as a distinguishing feature
  • Incidence ~1 in 10,000 live births; risk increases with maternal age
  • Most cases result from maternal nondisjunction in meiosis

Bottom Line: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) features holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, and cleft lip/palate - midline and digital abnormalities that distinguish it from other trisomies.

bio-497.subject: biology
bio-497.question: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) can result from Robertsonian translocation. In this scenario:
options: A piece of chromosome 21 attaches to chromosome 9, similar to the Philadelphia chromosome
Chromosome 21 is duplicated within itself, forming a ring chromosome
Both copies of chromosome 21 undergo complete deletion
The long arm of chromosome 21 is translocated to another acrocentric chromosome (often 14), giving the individual three functional copies of 21q genes despite having 46 chromosomes
bio-497.explanation:
Correct Answer: The long arm of chromosome 21 is translocated to another acrocentric chromosome (often 14), giving the individual three functional copies of 21q genes despite having 46 chromosomes

Robertsonian translocation involves the fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) at their centromeres, with loss of the short arms. In translocation Down syndrome, the most common form is t(14;21): the long arm of chromosome 21 is attached to chromosome 14. The individual has 46 chromosomes on karyotype but has three copies of the 21q genetic material (two normal 21s + one translocated 21q on chromosome 14), producing the Down syndrome phenotype.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. A piece of chromosome 21 attaches to chromosome 9, similar to the Philadelphia chromosome: The Philadelphia chromosome involves a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22). Robertsonian translocations specifically involve acrocentric chromosomes and are whole-arm fusions, not reciprocal exchanges. Chromosome 9 is not an acrocentric chromosome and does not participate in Robertsonian translocations.

B. Chromosome 21 is duplicated within itself, forming a ring chromosome: Ring chromosomes form when both ends of a chromosome are deleted and the remaining piece joins into a ring. This is a different structural abnormality and does not produce trisomy 21. Ring chromosome 21 can occur but typically causes partial monosomy, not trisomy.

C. Both copies of chromosome 21 undergo complete deletion: Deletion of both copies of chromosome 21 would be lethal (nullisomy). Down syndrome involves extra genetic material from chromosome 21, not loss of material.

Key Educational Points:

  • ~95% of Down syndrome = free trisomy 21 (nondisjunction); ~4% = Robertsonian translocation; ~1% = mosaicism
  • Translocation Down syndrome can be inherited from a balanced carrier parent
  • A balanced carrier of t(14;21) has 45 chromosomes and is phenotypically normal
  • Translocation Down syndrome is not associated with advanced maternal age (unlike free trisomy 21)

Bottom Line: Translocation Down syndrome results from Robertsonian translocation (usually 14;21), giving 46 chromosomes but three copies of 21q genetic material.

bio-498.subject: biology
bio-498.question: Amniocentesis is typically performed during which weeks of pregnancy?
options: Weeks 6–8
Weeks 10–12
Weeks 15–18
Weeks 28–32
bio-498.explanation:
Correct Answer: Weeks 15–18

Amniocentesis is typically performed between 15 and 18 weeks of gestation (second trimester). A needle is inserted through the mother's abdomen into the amniotic sac under ultrasound guidance, and ~20 mL of amniotic fluid is withdrawn. This fluid contains fetal cells (shed from the fetal skin, respiratory tract, and urinary tract) that can be cultured for karyotyping, biochemical analysis, or DNA testing. Results typically take 1–2 weeks due to the need to culture cells.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Weeks 6–8: At 6–8 weeks, the amniotic cavity is too small and contains insufficient amniotic fluid for safe sampling. At this early stage, the embryo is still very small and the procedure would carry an unacceptable risk. No prenatal invasive testing is routinely performed this early.

B. Weeks 10–12: This is the timing for chorionic villus sampling (CVS), not amniocentesis. CVS is performed between 10 and 13 weeks and samples placental tissue (chorionic villi) rather than amniotic fluid. CVS provides results earlier than amniocentesis but cannot test for neural tube defects (no α-fetoprotein measurement).

D. Weeks 28–32: By weeks 28–32, the pregnancy is in the third trimester. While late amniocentesis is sometimes performed for specific indications (e.g., assessing fetal lung maturity), routine diagnostic genetic testing via amniocentesis is done in the second trimester to allow time for decision-making.

Key Educational Points:

FeatureAmniocentesisCVS
Timing15–18 weeks10–13 weeks
SampleAmniotic fluid (fetal cells)Chorionic villi (placental tissue)
Risk of miscarriage~0.1–0.3%~0.5–1%
Neural tube defect testingYes (AFP in fluid)No
Results timing1–2 weeks1–2 weeks

Bottom Line: Amniocentesis is performed at 15–18 weeks of gestation; CVS is performed earlier at 10–13 weeks.

bio-499.subject: biology
bio-499.question: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has an advantage over amniocentesis in that it:
options: can be performed earlier in pregnancy (10–13 weeks vs. 15–18 weeks)
can detect neural tube defects through α-fetoprotein measurement
carries zero risk of miscarriage
requires no ultrasound guidance for the procedure
bio-499.explanation:
Correct Answer: can be performed earlier in pregnancy (10–13 weeks vs. 15–18 weeks)

The main advantage of CVS over amniocentesis is earlier timing: CVS is performed at 10–13 weeks of gestation, while amniocentesis is performed at 15–18 weeks. This allows earlier diagnosis and, if needed, earlier decision-making. CVS samples chorionic villi (placental tissue of fetal origin), which are rapidly dividing and can provide karyotype results without the extended cell culture required for amniocentesis.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B. Can detect neural tube defects through α-fetoprotein measurement: This is actually an advantage of amniocentesis, NOT CVS. Amniocentesis can measure α-fetoprotein (AFP) levels in amniotic fluid to screen for neural tube defects (such as spina bifida and anencephaly). CVS cannot assess AFP levels because it samples placental tissue, not amniotic fluid.

C. Carries zero risk of miscarriage: No invasive prenatal procedure carries zero risk. CVS actually has a slightly higher miscarriage risk (~0.5–1%) compared to amniocentesis (~0.1–0.3%). This is one of the trade-offs of earlier testing.

D. Requires no ultrasound guidance for the procedure: Both CVS and amniocentesis require real-time ultrasound guidance to ensure accurate needle/catheter placement and to avoid harming the fetus. Performing either procedure without ultrasound would be unsafe and is not standard practice.

Key Educational Points:

  • CVS can be done transcervically or transabdominally
  • A rare complication of very early CVS (before 10 weeks) is limb deficiency - which is why it is not performed before 10 weeks
  • Confined placental mosaicism (~1–2% of CVS results) can give misleading results, requiring follow-up amniocentesis

Bottom Line: CVS's main advantage is earlier timing (10–13 weeks vs. 15–18 weeks for amniocentesis), allowing earlier prenatal genetic diagnosis.

bio-500.subject: biology
bio-500.question: Two healthy parents each carry one copy of a recessive allele for cystic fibrosis (both are heterozygous carriers, Cc). What is the probability that their next child will be affected?
options: 0% - both parents are healthy
bio-500.explanation:
Correct Answer: 25%

When both parents are heterozygous carriers (Cc × Cc), the Punnett square gives the following offspring ratios: 1/4 CC (homozygous normal), 2/4 Cc (carrier), and 1/4 cc (affected). Therefore, there is a 25% (1 in 4) chance that any given child will be affected with cystic fibrosis.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. 0% - both parents are healthy: Being healthy does not mean both parents cannot produce affected children. Carriers of autosomal recessive diseases are phenotypically normal because one functional allele is sufficient for normal protein production. However, if both parents pass their recessive allele to a child, that child will be homozygous recessive (cc) and affected.

C. 50%: 50% is the probability that a child will be a CARRIER (Cc), not affected. A 50% risk of being affected would apply if one parent were affected (cc) and the other a carrier (Cc) - in that cross, 50% would be cc (affected) and 50% Cc (carrier).

D. 75%: 75% represents the fraction of offspring that are phenotypically normal (CC + Cc) in a Cc × Cc cross. This is the chance of being UNAFFECTED, not affected. It is a common mistake to confuse the affected and unaffected proportions.

Key Educational Points:

  • Autosomal recessive disease requires two copies of the mutant allele (homozygous recessive)
  • Carrier × Carrier → 25% affected, 50% carriers, 25% homozygous normal
  • Cystic fibrosis carrier frequency is ~1 in 25 among Caucasians
  • Each pregnancy is an independent event - prior children's status does not change the 25% probability

Bottom Line: When both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive disease, each child has a 25% chance of being affected.

bio-501.subject: biology
bio-501.question: Newborn screening for phenylketonuria (PKU) is performed routinely because:
options: PKU can be cured by gene therapy immediately after birth
Early detection allows dietary modification (restricting phenylalanine) that prevents intellectual disability
PKU is an X-linked disorder that only affects males and needs early hormone treatment
The PKU screening test can also detect all other metabolic disorders simultaneously
bio-501.explanation:
Correct Answer: Early detection allows dietary modification (restricting phenylalanine) that prevents intellectual disability

PKU is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Without treatment, phenylalanine accumulates and causes severe intellectual disability, seizures, musty body odor, and light skin/hair pigmentation. Newborn screening using the Guthrie test or tandem mass spectrometry detects elevated phenylalanine levels in blood. Early initiation of a low-phenylalanine diet (within the first weeks of life) prevents neurological damage and allows normal development.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. PKU can be cured by gene therapy immediately after birth: Gene therapy for PKU is currently under research but is not yet a standard clinical treatment. The primary treatment remains lifelong dietary restriction of phenylalanine. Some patients also benefit from sapropterin (BH4 supplementation), but this is not gene therapy.

C. PKU is an X-linked disorder that only affects males: PKU is autosomal recessive, NOT X-linked. Both males and females are affected equally. The PAH gene is located on chromosome 12. X-linked disorders preferentially affect males (e.g., hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy), but PKU is not one of them.

D. The PKU screening test can also detect all other metabolic disorders simultaneously: While modern tandem mass spectrometry newborn screening panels can detect many metabolic disorders simultaneously, this is NOT the reason PKU screening was originally implemented. PKU screening was one of the first newborn screens established because it met the criteria: the disease is common enough, detectable before symptoms, and treatable if caught early.

Key Educational Points:

  • PKU screening was the first newborn screening test (Robert Guthrie, 1960s)
  • Criteria for newborn screening: common, detectable presymptomatically, treatable, and screening is cost-effective
  • Maternal PKU: women with PKU who do not control phenylalanine during pregnancy can cause birth defects in their children (even if the child does not have PKU)

Bottom Line: Newborn PKU screening enables early dietary intervention that prevents irreversible intellectual disability - a model for successful newborn screening programs.

bio-502.subject: biology
bio-502.question: A pedigree shows an affected father who has ALL affected daughters and NO affected sons. The mother is unaffected. What is the most likely inheritance pattern?
options: Autosomal recessive
Autosomal dominant
X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
bio-502.explanation:
Correct Answer: X-linked dominant

When an affected father has an X-linked dominant trait, ALL of his daughters will be affected because they all receive his X chromosome carrying the dominant disease allele (XDY father × XdXd mother → daughters are all XDXd, affected). None of his sons will be affected because sons receive their father's Y chromosome, not his X (sons are all XdY, unaffected).

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Autosomal recessive: If the father is affected (aa) and the mother is unaffected, the children would depend on the mother's genotype. If the mother is AA, no children would be affected. If she is Aa, 50% would be carriers and 50% affected. Autosomal recessive does not show the sex-specific pattern described (all daughters affected, no sons affected).

B. Autosomal dominant: An affected autosomal dominant father (Aa) crossed with an unaffected mother (aa) would produce 50% affected and 50% unaffected children, regardless of sex. It would NOT preferentially affect all daughters and no sons.

D. X-linked recessive: An X-linked recessive affected father (XaY) crossed with an unaffected carrier mother would produce affected sons and carrier daughters. But if the mother is homozygous normal (XAXA), ALL daughters would be carriers (XAXa, unaffected) and all sons would be unaffected (XAY). An affected father with X-linked recessive cannot produce affected daughters unless the mother is at least a carrier.

Key Educational Points:

  • X-linked dominant: affected father → ALL daughters affected, NO sons affected
  • X-linked dominant: affected mother → 50% sons and 50% daughters affected
  • Examples of X-linked dominant disorders: Rett syndrome, hypophosphatemic rickets, Aicardi syndrome

Bottom Line: An affected father with ALL affected daughters and NO affected sons indicates X-linked dominant inheritance - every daughter gets his single X chromosome.

bio-503.subject: biology
bio-503.question: A couple is told that their karyotype analysis shows a balanced reciprocal translocation in the father. He is phenotypically normal. What should the genetic counselor explain about the implications?
options: Balanced translocations never cause problems in offspring
The father's fertility is unaffected, and all children will be normal
Although the father is normal, there is an increased risk of unbalanced chromosomal arrangements in offspring, which can cause miscarriages or birth defects
The father must have a chromosomal disorder that has not yet manifested
bio-503.explanation:
Correct Answer: Although the father is normal, there is an increased risk of unbalanced chromosomal arrangements in offspring, which can cause miscarriages or birth defects

A balanced translocation carrier has no net gain or loss of genetic material, so they are usually phenotypically normal. However, during meiosis, the translocated chromosomes must segregate into gametes. Depending on how the chromosomes segregate (alternate, adjacent-1, adjacent-2, or 3:1), some gametes will be unbalanced - having duplications or deletions of chromosomal segments. Fertilization with these unbalanced gametes can result in miscarriage, stillbirth, or liveborn children with congenital abnormalities.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. Balanced translocations never cause problems in offspring: This is incorrect and would be dangerous genetic counseling. While the carrier is normal, their offspring are at significant risk for unbalanced chromosomal arrangements. The risk varies depending on the specific chromosomes involved and the segregation pattern.

B. The father's fertility is unaffected, and all children will be normal: Balanced translocation carriers often experience reduced fertility due to high rates of miscarriage from unbalanced gametes. Not all children will be normal - they can be: (1) chromosomally normal, (2) balanced carriers like the father, or (3) unbalanced (partial trisomy/monosomy).

D. The father must have a chromosomal disorder that has not yet manifested: Balanced translocation carriers are typically truly normal because they have the complete genome - just rearranged. They do not have a hidden disorder waiting to manifest. The issue is with meiotic segregation in their gametes, not with their own phenotype.

Key Educational Points:

  • Balanced translocation carriers: normal phenotype, risk to offspring
  • This is one of the most common indications for genetic counseling in couples with recurrent pregnancy loss
  • Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) can be used with IVF to select embryos with normal or balanced chromosome complements

Bottom Line: Balanced translocation carriers are phenotypically normal but have an increased risk of producing offspring with unbalanced chromosomal arrangements causing miscarriage or birth defects.

bio-504.subject: biology
bio-504.question: Which of the following is an ethical consideration unique to predictive genetic testing (e.g., testing for Huntington disease in an asymptomatic person)?
options: The test may produce false-negative results due to lab error
The test results may cause psychological harm, affect insurance eligibility, and reveal information about family members who may not wish to know their status
Predictive testing is not covered by any guidelines or regulations
Positive results always lead to immediate and effective treatment
bio-504.explanation:
Correct Answer: The test results may cause psychological harm, affect insurance eligibility, and reveal information about family members who may not wish to know their status

Predictive genetic testing for late-onset conditions like Huntington disease (HD) raises complex ethical issues: (1) psychological impact - learning one carries the HD gene (with 100% penetrance) when no cure exists can cause severe anxiety, depression, or suicidal ideation; (2) insurance discrimination - genetic information may be used by insurers or employers; (3) family implications - a positive result in one family member implies that a parent is also a carrier and siblings have a 50% risk, even if those family members have not consented to learn this information.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. The test may produce false-negative results due to lab error: While laboratory errors can occur with any test, this is not an ethical issue unique to predictive genetic testing. False-negative results are a general concern in all diagnostic testing, not a specific ethical dilemma of presymptomatic genetic testing.

C. Predictive testing is not covered by any guidelines or regulations: Predictive genetic testing IS covered by guidelines and regulations. In many countries, laws like GINA (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act) in the US provide some protections. Professional organizations have established detailed protocols for predictive testing, especially for conditions like Huntington disease.

D. Positive results always lead to immediate and effective treatment: For many conditions tested predictively (like Huntington disease), there is currently no cure or effective treatment. This is actually part of the ethical dilemma - is it beneficial to inform someone of a condition for which no treatment exists? This statement is factually incorrect.

Key Educational Points:

  • Huntington disease testing protocol requires pre-test and post-test genetic counseling
  • Testing of minors for adult-onset conditions is generally not recommended unless there is a medical intervention available
  • The right NOT to know one's genetic status is recognized as an ethical principle

Bottom Line: Predictive genetic testing raises unique ethical issues including psychological harm, insurance discrimination, and unconsented disclosure of family members' genetic status.

bio-505.subject: biology
bio-505.question: Congenital hypothyroidism is included in newborn screening programs because:
options: It is an autosomal dominant condition that is easy to diagnose clinically at birth
Early thyroid hormone replacement prevents irreversible intellectual disability and growth failure
It only affects premature infants and resolves spontaneously
The treatment requires surgical intervention within 48 hours of birth
bio-505.explanation:
Correct Answer: Early thyroid hormone replacement prevents irreversible intellectual disability and growth failure

Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) occurs in ~1 in 3,000 newborns and is one of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability. If untreated, thyroid hormone deficiency during the critical period of brain development leads to cretinism (irreversible intellectual disability, short stature, coarse facial features). Newborn screening detects elevated TSH (or low T4), and early initiation of levothyroxine (synthetic T4) replacement within the first 2 weeks of life leads to normal cognitive development.

Why the other choices are wrong:

A. It is an autosomal dominant condition that is easy to diagnose clinically at birth: Congenital hypothyroidism is usually NOT clinically apparent at birth - most newborns appear normal initially. Symptoms develop gradually over weeks to months. This is precisely why screening is necessary: by the time clinical signs appear, irreversible brain damage may have occurred. Also, most cases are due to thyroid dysgenesis (sporadic), not simple autosomal dominant inheritance.

C. It only affects premature infants and resolves spontaneously: CH affects both term and preterm infants.
